interactions.label: A 30-year-old woman presents with a red right eye. The redness is brightest away

params.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with a red right eye. The redness is brightest away from the cornea and blanches on gentle pressure. She reports watery discharge and mild grittiness but no photophobia, no pain, and normal vision. Based on the pattern of redness and the absence of danger signs, which anatomical structure is most likely the source of inflammation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Corneal involvement (keratitis) typically produces ciliary flush — a non-blanching violet ring around the corneal margin — along with pain and photophobia. The blanching injection pattern here, worst away from the cornea with no danger signs, points to a more superficial structure.

Correct! Bright red redness worst away from the cornea that blanches on pressure is conjunctival injection, localising inflammation to the conjunctiva. The absence of all five danger signs (Pain, Photophobia, Pupil abnormality, vision Change, Corneal opacity/Ciliary flush) confirms this is not sight-threatening.

Uveal inflammation (anterior uveitis) presents with ciliary flush — a deep violet non-blanching ring around the cornea — along with photophobia and often a constricted or irregular pupil. The blanching injection pattern and normal vision here are inconsistent with uveitis.
Scleritis causes deep boring pain and a violaceous hue that does not blanch on pressure. The blanching, bright red injection and absence of pain here rule out scleral involvement.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key analysis: redness brightest away from the cornea that blanches on pressure = conjunctival injection. Then cross-check PPPCC (Pain, Photophobia, Pupil abnormality, vision Change, Corneal opacity/Ciliary flush) — all absent. This localises inflammation to the conjunctiva, not deeper structures.
You correctly analysed the injection pattern and danger-sign profile to localise inflammation. Conjunctival injection that blanches + zero PPPCC signs = conjunctivitis, not a sight-threatening cause.

params.question: A 22-year-old man presents with acute onset of copious purulent discharge from the right eye. On wiping, the discharge reforms within seconds. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

answers.text: Topical chloramphenicol eye drops four times daily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Discharge reforming within seconds of wiping indicates hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis — a sight-threatening emergency. Topical antibiotics alone cannot prevent corneal perforation; systemic treatment is essential.
Single-dose oral azithromycin is the treatment for chlamydial conjunctivitis. Hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis requires systemic ceftriaxone to prevent corneal perforation.

Correct! Discharge reforming within seconds of wiping is the hallmark of hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis. Systemic ceftriaxone is required immediately because topical treatment alone cannot prevent corneal perforation.

answers.text: Warm compresses and lubricant drops with review in one week

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is a sight-threatening emergency, not a self-limiting condition. Gonococcal conjunctivitis can perforate the cornea within hours — watchful waiting risks permanent visual loss.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical clue is discharge reforming within seconds of wiping — this identifies hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis, an emergency requiring systemic ceftriaxone. Topical antibiotics alone are insufficient to prevent corneal perforation.
You recognised the hallmark of gonococcal conjunctivitis — hyperacute discharge that reforms within seconds — and chose appropriate systemic treatment to prevent corneal perforation.

interactions.label: A 45-year-old woman with trachomatous trichiasis (grade TT) has her lashes abrad

params.question: A 45-year-old woman with trachomatous trichiasis (grade TT) has her lashes abrading her cornea. Her active chlamydial infection was cleared with azithromycin, yet her corneal damage continues to worsen. Which component of the SAFE strategy directly addresses her ongoing problem?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Her active infection has already been cleared. The ongoing damage is mechanical — scarred tarsal conjunctiva has turned her eyelid inward, causing lashes to scrape the cornea with every blink. Antibiotics cannot reverse established structural scarring.
Facial cleanliness prevents transmission of active disease by removing the discharge that attracts Musca sorbens flies. It cannot address the mechanical damage from established cicatricial entropion.

Correct! Once trachomatous scarring causes cicatricial entropion with trichiasis, each blink deepens corneal damage. Bilamellar tarsal rotation is a lid-splitting procedure that corrects the eyelid position and turns lashes away from the cornea — the only SAFE component that addresses irreversible structural damage.
Latrines and clean water access reduce Musca sorbens breeding and prevent trachoma transmission. They cannot correct the established entropion that is mechanically damaging her cornea.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle: once trachomatous scarring (grade TT) causes cicatricial entropion with trichiasis, the damage is mechanical — lashes abrade the cornea with every blink. Antibiotics, facial cleanliness, and environmental measures prevent new infection but cannot reverse structural scarring. Only surgery (bilamellar tarsal rotation) corrects the lid deformity.
You correctly identified that once trachoma has caused structural scarring (grade TT), surgical correction is the only SAFE component that can halt ongoing mechanical corneal damage.

interactions.label: The shield ulcer in vernal keratoconjunctivitis is caused by bacterial infection

params.question: The shield ulcer in vernal keratoconjunctivitis is caused by bacterial infection of the cornea and should be treated with intensive topical antibiotics.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The shield ulcer looks like an infective corneal ulcer but is actually caused by eosinophil toxicity, not bacteria. The video specifically warns: treating it as bacterial keratitis causes dangerous corneal scarring. Understanding this distinction prevents a harmful management error.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct! The shield ulcer is NOT infective — it is a superficial oval corneal erosion caused by toxic proteins released from eosinophils, not bacteria. Treating it as bacterial keratitis with aggressive antibiotics causes dangerous corneal scarring. The underlying allergic inflammation must be addressed instead.

params.question: A 50-year-old outdoor worker has a nasal wing-shaped growth on his right eye. A probe cannot pass beneath the neck at the limbus, and the head of the growth is 2 mm from the pupillary margin. Which surgical approach offers the lowest recurrence rate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: With the growth head only 2 mm from the pupil — within the 3 mm surgical threshold — surgery is indicated. Observation alone risks further corneal encroachment and progressive irregular astigmatism.
Bare sclera excision carries a recurrence rate of 50–80%. Although excision is correctly indicated here, this technique alone is inferior when a better alternative exists.

Correct! The probe test confirms true pterygium (probe cannot pass beneath the neck). With the head 2 mm from the pupil (within the 3 mm threshold), surgery is indicated. Conjunctival autograft brings recurrence below 10%, far superior to the 50–80% rate with bare sclera excision.

Medical treatment cannot reverse a pterygium once it has encroached onto the cornea. With the head within 3 mm of the pupil, surgical excision with conjunctival autograft is the appropriate management.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key facts: the probe test (cannot pass beneath the neck) confirms true pterygium. When the head is within 3 mm of the pupil, surgery is indicated. Conjunctival autograft gives <10% recurrence, versus 50–80% with bare sclera excision.

You correctly identified the surgical indication (head ≤3 mm from pupil), confirmed true pterygium via the probe test, and chose the technique with the lowest recurrence rate — conjunctival autograft (<10%).

params.question: A patient newly prescribed timolol drops and an antibiotic ointment asks how to use both medications correctly. Which instruction is correct?

answers.text: Apply the ointment first, then instil the drops after five minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ointments must always be applied LAST, after all drops. An ointment applied first coats the ocular surface with an oily film and prevents subsequent drops from being properly absorbed.

answers.text: Instil both medications together to save time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Instilling medications together causes the first to be washed out by the second. Different drops must be spaced five minutes apart for adequate absorption, and ointments always go last.

answers.text: Instil the drops first, wait five minutes, then apply the ointment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Drops are always instilled first, with at least five minutes between different drops to allow adequate absorption. Ointments go last because their oily base would block absorption of any subsequent drops.

answers.text: Press the outer corner of the eye for two minutes after each drop

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nasolacrimal occlusion is performed by pressing the INNER corner (medial canthus), not the outer corner, for one to two minutes. This blocks the nasolacrimal duct and reduces systemic absorption — critical for drugs like timolol that can cause bronchospasm if absorbed systemically.

overallFeedback.feedback: The sequencing rule: instil drops first, wait five minutes between different drops, and always apply ointments last. Press the INNER corner (medial canthus) for one to two minutes after each drop to block nasolacrimal drainage and reduce systemic absorption.

You correctly applied the instillation rules: drops before ointments, five-minute spacing between different drops. Poor technique is the most modifiable factor in treatment compliance — up to 50% of glaucoma patients stop using drops correctly within twelve months.
